title: Financial Services Regulation: A Briefing Programme for Parliamentarians
summary: A six-module, non-technical briefing programme helping parliamentarians and committee staff scrutinise financial legislation and hold regulators to account.
intro: This training programme equips parliamentarians and committee staff with a clear, non-technical understanding of how financial regulation works, so they can scrutinise legislation, hold regulators to account and respond to emerging issues with confidence.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give legislators and their staff a concise, jargon-free briefing on financial services regulation, the role of independent regulators and the issues that come before parliament. Participants leave able to ask incisive questions of regulators and ministers, scrutinise financial legislation effectively and judge emerging issues such as crypto-assets and AI.
sections.What It Covers: How financial regulation works and who does what, holding independent regulators to account, scrutinising financial legislation, consumer protection and lessons from financial scandals, financial crime and the country's international obligations, and emerging issues including crypto-assets and AI.
Intended Audience: Members of parliament, particularly those on finance, economic affairs, budget and public accounts committees
Committee clerks, researchers and parliamentary library staff supporting financial scrutiny
Advisers to parliamentarians and party policy staff working on financial issues
Learning Objectives: Explain in plain language why financial services are regulated and who does what
Hold regulators to account while respecting their operational independence
Scrutinise financial legislation and the powers it confers
Draw lessons from financial scandals for consumer protection policy
Explain the country's financial crime obligations and how they are assessed internationally
Ask informed questions about emerging issues such as crypto-assets and AI
sections.Structure and Format: Six modules of about two hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a two-day programme or as a series of short briefing sessions around the parliamentary timetable. Each module combines a plain-language briefing with a case study and a scrutiny question set, and modules can be selected or tailored to committee priorities.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: No prior knowledge of financial services or regulation is required. Experience of committee work is helpful.
Core Reading: OECD (2014), The Governance of Regulators, OECD Best Practice Principles for Regulatory Policy
G20/OECD (2022), High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection
FATF (2012, updated), International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations
IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation

modules.title: How Financial Regulation Works
modules.summary: Why financial services are regulated, the institutions responsible, and how international standards shape national rules, explained without jargon.
objectives: Explain the purposes of financial regulation
Identify the roles of the ministry, central bank, regulators and other bodies
Describe how international standards influence national law
syllabus: What can go wrong in finance and why it matters to constituents
Who regulates what: the national regulatory map
International standard-setters and peer reviews
Key terms every legislator should know

modules.title: Holding Regulators to Account
modules.summary: Why regulators are given independence, the accountability mechanisms parliament controls, and how to conduct effective scrutiny hearings and inquiries.
objectives: Explain the rationale for regulatory independence and its limits
Use annual reports, hearings and inquiries to scrutinise regulators
Distinguish legitimate scrutiny from interference in individual cases
syllabus: Independence, mandates and appointments
Annual reports, budgets and performance information
Preparing for and conducting a scrutiny hearing
A question set for regulators and ministers

modules.title: Scrutinising Financial Legislation
modules.summary: How financial bills are structured, what to look for in the powers and safeguards they contain, and how to test impact assessments and industry claims.
objectives: Identify the main components of a financial services bill
Assess delegated powers, safeguards and review clauses
Test impact assessments, consultation responses and lobbying claims
syllabus: Perimeter, licensing, enforcement and transitional provisions explained
Delegated powers and parliamentary oversight of rules
Reading an impact assessment critically
Engaging with industry and consumer representations

modules.title: Consumer Protection and Lessons from Scandals
modules.summary: How consumer protection in finance is meant to work, what recent mis-selling and fraud scandals reveal about regulatory failure, and the remedies available to consumers.
objectives: Describe the main consumer protection tools and redress mechanisms
Draw lessons from mis-selling and fraud scandals
Assess whether consumers can obtain effective redress
syllabus: Disclosure, suitability, fair treatment and product rules
Case studies of mis-selling, investment fraud and firm failures
Ombudsman schemes, compensation and deposit protection
Constituency casework: helping consumers who have lost money

modules.title: Financial Crime and International Obligations
modules.summary: The country's obligations to combat money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion, how they are assessed by the FATF, and what is at stake for the economy.
objectives: Explain the FATF standards and the mutual evaluation process
Describe the consequences of grey-listing for the economy
Identify the legislative role in beneficial ownership and asset recovery
syllabus: Money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions explained
FATF evaluations, grey-listing and its economic impact
Beneficial ownership transparency and asset recovery laws
Scams and fraud as a growing financial crime threat

modules.title: Emerging Issues: Crypto-Assets, AI and the Future of Finance
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining emerging issues likely to come before parliament, including crypto-assets, stablecoins, AI, climate risk and cyber threats.
objectives: Explain crypto-assets, stablecoins and AI in plain language
Assess the main risks and regulatory options for emerging issues
Prepare a scrutiny agenda for the parliamentary term
syllabus: Crypto-assets and stablecoins: risks and regulatory approaches
AI in finance: benefits, risks and accountability
Climate risk, cyber threats and operational resilience
Workshop: a committee scrutiny agenda on financial services

related.title: Building a Competitive Financial Centre: Strategy, Regulation and Investment Promotion
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping ministries and investment promotion agencies build a competitive, reputable financial centre and measure the results.

related.title: Drafting Financial Services Legislation
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping legislative drafters and legal advisers design and draft effective, enforceable and technology-neutral financial services legislation.

related.title: Financial Crises and Public Finances: Crisis Preparedness for Government
related.summary: An eight-module advanced programme preparing finance ministries and senior officials to manage financial crises, protect public finances and coordinate resolution.

related.title: Financial Services Policy Essentials for Government
related.summary: A ten-module programme giving government officials a clear grounding in the financial system, regulatory architecture, international standards and the policy levers government holds.

related.title: AI in Financial Services: Policy Choices for Government
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping policymakers understand AI in financial services and make informed choices on regulation, institutional roles and national strategy.

related.title: Developing Capital Markets and Investment Fund Industries
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping policymakers develop deep, well-regulated capital markets and fund industries through credible, well-sequenced reform.
